SAT Math 3.5 — Two-Variable Data & Models

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Describing a scatterplot

say three things: direction (up or down) | strength (tight or scattered) | form (straight or curved)

Direction is whether y rises or falls as x rises. Strength is how closely the points hug a line. Form is whether that pattern is a line at all — a tight parabola is a strong association but not a linear one. The SAT asks you to name all three, and a strong curve is the classic trap.

Example 1. Points rise from bottom-left to top-right and lie very close to a line. Describe the association.
Solution.

Strong positive linear association. Rising is positive, hugging the line is strong, straight is linear.

Example 2. Points fall as x rises but are widely scattered. Describe it.
Solution.

Weak negative linear association. Falling is negative; the scatter makes it weak.

Example 3. Points rise, level off, then fall, forming a tight arch. Is this a strong linear association?
Solution.

No. It is a strong association but not a linear one.

Strength and form are separate judgements, and a line of best fit would describe this badly.

2The line of best fit

the line of best fit minimises the total squared vertical distance | in Desmos type y₁~mx₁+b under a table

The line does not have to pass through any data point, and usually passes through none. Its slope is the predicted change in y for a one-unit rise in x, and its y-intercept is the predicted y when x is zero — which may be meaningless in context.

Example 1. For the data (1, 5), (2, 8), (3, 10), (4, 14), Desmos reports y = 2.9x + 2. What does 2.9 mean?
Solution.

For every increase of 1 in x, the model predicts y rises by about 2.9.

Example 2. What does the intercept 2 mean in that model?
Solution.

It is the predicted value of y when x = 0, so about 2.

If x = 0 is outside the data range, this is extrapolation and may have no sensible meaning.

Example 3. Does the line pass through (3, 10)?
Solution.

At x = 3 the line gives 2.9(3) + 2 = 10.7, not 10.

No — a line of best fit need not pass through any data point.

3Predicting from a model

substitute the x you are given | inside the data range is interpolation, outside is extrapolation

Prediction is just substitution. The judgement the SAT tests is whether the prediction is trustworthy: inside the range of the data it usually is; far outside it, the model has no evidence behind it and the prediction is unreliable however neat the arithmetic.

Example 1. Using y = 2.9x + 2, predict y when x = 4.
Solution.

2.9(4) + 2 = 11.6 + 2 = 13.6.

Example 2. The data covers x from 1 to 4. How much should you trust a prediction at x = 30?
Solution.

Very little. x = 30 is far outside the data, so this is extrapolation — the model has no evidence that the pattern continues that far.

Example 3. Using y = 2.9x + 2, for what x does the model predict y = 25?
Solution.

2.9x + 2 = 25, so 2.9x = 23 and x = 23/2.9 ≈ 7.93.

4Residuals

residual = actual − predicted | positive means the point sits above the line

A residual measures one point’s miss. Subtract in that order every time: actual first. A residual plot with no pattern says a line was the right model; a residual plot with a curve says it was not.

Example 1. The model predicts 13.6 and the actual value is 14. Find the residual.
Solution.

14 − 13.6 = +0.4. Positive, so the point lies just above the line.

Example 2. The model predicts 10.7 and the actual value is 10. Find the residual.
Solution.

10 − 10.7 = −0.7. Negative, so this point lies below the line.

Example 3. A residual plot shows a clear U shape. What does that tell you?
Solution.

The straight-line model is not appropriate — the data curves, and a line systematically over- then under-predicts.

5Correlation is not causation

an association shows two things move together | only a randomised experiment shows one causes the other

This is tested in words, not numbers. However strong the association, an observational study cannot establish cause. Watch for a lurking third variable that drives both quantities.

Example 1. Ice-cream sales and swimming accidents rise together. Does ice cream cause accidents?
Solution.

No. Hot weather raises both — a lurking variable.

The association is real; the causal claim is not.

Example 2. A study finds students who own more books score higher. Can the school conclude books raise scores?
Solution.

No. This is observational, so it shows association only.

Family income could drive both.

Example 3. What would be needed to support a causal claim?
Solution.

A randomised controlled experiment: assign students to conditions at random, so the groups differ only in the treatment.

6Exponential against linear growth

constant difference → linear | constant ratio → exponential

Check the table before choosing a model. Subtract consecutive y-values: if those differences are about equal, the model is linear. Divide consecutive y-values instead: if those ratios are about equal, it is exponential. Exponential growth eventually overtakes any linear growth.

Example 1. y goes 3, 7, 11, 15 as x goes 1, 2, 3, 4. Which model fits?
Solution.

Differences 4, 4, 4 are constant, so the model is linear, y = 4x − 1.

Example 2. y goes 3, 6, 12, 24. Which model fits?
Solution.

Ratios 2, 2, 2 are constant, so the model is exponential, y = 1.5(2)ˣ.

Example 3. y goes 100, 90, 81, 72.9. Linear or exponential?
Solution.

Differences −10, −9, −8.1 are not constant, but ratios are all 0.9.

Exponential decay, falling 10% each step.

Part 1 — With Desmos (10 questions · every one is faster on the graph)

The SAT gives you Desmos on every maths question. This is the one data topic where Desmos really earns its place: type a table and the regression line y₁~mx₁+b, and it reports the slope and intercept directly.

#QuestionType into DesmosThenAnswer

D2For that same data, what is the y-intercept of the line of best fit?y_1~mx_1+bDesmos reports m and b together.2
D3Using y = 2.9x + 2, what value does the model predict when x = 4?2.9*4+2Substitute and let Desmos evaluate.13.6
D4The actual value at x = 4 is 14 and the model predicts 13.6. What is the residual?14-(2.9*4+2)Actual minus predicted, in that order.0.4
D5Using y = 2.9x + 2, for what value of x does the model predict y = 25? Round to two decimal places.(25-2)/2.9Solve the linear equation in one line.7.93

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Three things get tested: what the slope and intercept mean, how far the model may be trusted, and what the data does and does not let you claim.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
The scatterplot shows four data points and the line of best fit y = 2.9x + 2. What value does the model predict when x = 4?
13.6

2.9(4) + 2 = 11.6 + 2 = 13.6.

A common wrong answer drops the intercept; C is the actual data value, not the prediction.

P2Hard
For the data shown, the line of best fit is y = 2.9x + 2 and the actual value at x = 4 is 14. What is the residual at x = 4?
0.4

Residual = actual − predicted = 14 − 13.6 = 0.4.

Positive, so the point sits above the line.

P3Hard
A scatterplot of hours studied against test score shows points rising steeply and lying very close to a straight line. Which best describes the association?
Strong positive linear

Rising is positive; points close to the line make it strong; straight makes it linear.

Strong positive linear. A common wrong answer would need a visible curve.

P4Hard
In the model y = 2.9x + 2 relating x hours of training to y units produced, what is the best interpretation of 2.9?
The predicted rise in output for each extra hour of training.

A slope is a rate of change: per extra unit of x, y is predicted to rise by 2.9.

A common wrong answer describes the intercept.

P5Hard
A table shows y = 3, 6, 12, 24 as x = 1, 2, 3, 4. Which type of model best fits the data?
Exponential, because the ratios are constant

Differences are 3, 6, 12 — not constant. Ratios are 2, 2, 2 — constant.

A constant ratio means exponential. The pairing of reason to conclusion is what is being tested.

P6Hard
A town's population of 1200 decreases by 8% each year. To the nearest whole number, what is the population after 5 years?
791

A fall of 8% multiplies by 0.92 each year.

1200(0.92)⁵ = 790.89… ≈ 791. Subtracting 8% of 1200 five times would give 720, which is the common error.

P7Very
hard
A study finds that towns with more bookshops have higher average exam results. State the best-supported conclusion.
There is an association, but a third factor such as household income may explain both.

The study is observational, so it supports association only. A lurking variable such as income can raise both.

A causal claim would need random assignment, which no town study can provide.

P8Very
hard
For a set of data the line of best fit is y = 2.9x + 2. At x = 3 the actual value is 10. What is the residual, and what does its sign mean?
−0.7; the point is below the line

Predicted = 2.9(3) + 2 = 10.7. Residual = 10 − 10.7 = −0.7.

Negative means the actual value is below the prediction. A common wrong answer reverses the subtraction.

P9Very
hard
The data used to build the model y = 2.9x + 2 covers x from 1 to 4. A manager uses it to predict the value at x = 30. Which is the best criticism?
x = 30 is far outside the data range, so the prediction is unreliable.

2.9(30) + 2 = 89 is arithmetically fine, but x = 30 is well beyond the evidence.

This is extrapolation, and nothing in the data shows the pattern continues.

P10Very
hard
A residual plot for a linear model shows the residuals forming a clear U shape rather than scattering randomly. What does this indicate?
A linear model is not appropriate for this data.

A pattern in the residuals means the model is missing structure in the data.

A line is the wrong model here — the relationship curves. A good residual plot looks like random scatter about zero.

P11Very
hard
Two quantities are recorded: y = 100, 90, 81, 72.9 as x = 0, 1, 2, 3. A student says the data is linear because y keeps falling by about the same amount. Why is the student wrong, and what model fits?
The differences are −10, −9, −8.1, which are not constant; the ratios are all 0.9, so the model is exponential decay.

Differences −10, −9, −8.1 shrink; ratios 90/100 = 81/90 = 72.9/81 = 0.9 are constant.

A constant ratio below 1 is exponential decay, a 10% fall each step. Over a short run a decay curve can look almost straight, which is exactly the trap.

P12Very
hard
Data points (2, 11) and (6, 23) lie on a line of best fit. What does the model predict at x = 10?
35

Slope = (23 − 11)/(6 − 2) = 12/4 = 3, and 11 = 3(2) + b gives b = 5.

At x = 10: 3(10) + 5 = 35.

The one habit to build. A line of best fit is evidence only inside the range it was built from, and only ever about association. Two of these twelve are answered by refusing to overclaim — and that refusal is the correct answer, not a dodge.

SAT Math 3.6 — Probability

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Basic probability

P(event) = favourable ÷ total | every probability lies between 0 and 1

Count what you want, count everything, divide. The commonest error is counting the total wrong — add all the categories, including the one you are not choosing. A probability above 1 always means the denominator is wrong.

Example 1. A bag holds 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green counters. What is P(blue)?
Solution.

Total = 5 + 4 + 3 = 12.

P(blue) = 4/12 = 1/3.

Example 2. For the same bag, what is P(not green)?
Solution.

Not green means red or blue: 5 + 4 = 9 of 12.

9/12 = 3/4. Equivalently 1 − 3/12.

Example 3. A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. What is P(a number greater than 5)?
Solution.

The values 6, 7, 8 qualify — three of them.

P = 3/8. ‘Greater than 5’ excludes 5 itself.

2Probability from a two-way table

decide the whole first: grand total, one row, or one column

Almost every two-way-table question is easy arithmetic and one hard decision — which total goes underneath. Read the sentence for the group being described; that group is the denominator.

Example 1. From the table above, what is the probability that a randomly chosen customer bought cheese?
Solution.

The Cheese column totals 60 + 20 = 80, out of 180.

P = 80/180 = 4/9.

Example 2. What is the probability that a customer bought both fruit and cheese?
Solution.

One cell, 60, out of the grand total 180.

P = 60/180 = 1/3.

Example 3. What is the probability that a customer bought fruit but not cheese?
Solution.

That cell holds 40, out of 180.

P = 40/180 = 2/9.

3Conditional probability

‘given that’ or ‘of those who’ → the named group becomes the whole

This is the highest-value idea in the topic and the one your class loses marks on. The phrase ‘of the customers who bought fruit’ replaces the grand total with the fruit row. Nothing else changes — the numerator is still the overlap.

Example 1. Of the customers who bought fruit, what is the probability one also bought cheese?
Solution.

The whole is now the Fruit row, 100.

P = 60/100 = 3/5, not 60/180.

Example 2. Given that a customer bought cheese, what is the probability they bought fruit?
Solution.

Now the whole is the Cheese column, 80.

P = 60/80 = 3/4. Notice this differs from the previous answer — order matters.

Example 3. Of the customers who did not buy fruit, what fraction bought cheese?
Solution.

The No-fruit row totals 20 + 60 = 80.

P = 20/80 = 1/4.

4Independent events and ‘and’

independent events: P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) | without replacement the second probability changes

Multiply along a sequence of events. The question to ask is whether the first event changes the second: drawing with replacement leaves the bag unchanged, drawing without replacement removes one item from both the numerator and the total.

Example 1. A fair coin is tossed twice. What is P(two heads)?
Solution.

The tosses are independent.

P = ½ × ½ = 1/4.

Example 2. A bag has 5 red and 3 blue. Two are drawn with replacement. What is P(both red)?
Solution.

The bag is unchanged between draws.

P = (5/8)(5/8) = 25/64.

Example 3. The same bag, but drawn without replacement. What is P(both red)?
Solution.

After one red is taken, 4 reds remain out of 7.

P = (5/8)(4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14.

5‘Or’ and the overlap

P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B)

Adding two probabilities double-counts anything in both, so subtract the overlap once. If the events cannot happen together, the overlap is zero and the formula collapses to simple addition.

Example 1. From the table, what is P(bought fruit or bought cheese)?
Solution.

100/180 + 80/180 − 60/180 = 120/180 = 2/3. Without subtracting the 60, you would wrongly get 1.

Example 2. A card is drawn from 52. What is P(a heart or a king)?
Solution.

13/52 + 4/52 − 1/52 (the king of hearts) = 16/52 = 4/13.

Example 3. A die is rolled. What is P(an even number or a 5)?
Solution.

Even gives 3 outcomes, 5 gives 1, and they cannot both happen.

P = 3/6 + 1/6 = 4/6 = 2/3.

6Expected counts

expected number = probability × group size

When a question scales a proportion up to a larger population, multiply. This is the same arithmetic as a percentage of a total, and the answer should be rounded to a whole number of people or items when that is what is being counted.

Example 1. The probability a customer buys cheese is 4/9. In a day with 450 customers, how many are expected to buy cheese?
Solution.

(4/9)(450) = 200 customers.

Example 2. A machine produces faulty parts 3% of the time. How many faults are expected in 1,200 parts?
Solution.

0.03 × 1200 = 36 parts.

Example 3. In a survey, 60 of 100 fruit buyers also bought cheese. In a town with 2,500 fruit buyers, how many are expected to buy cheese?
Solution.

The rate is 60/100 = 0.6.

0.6 × 2500 = 1,500 people.

Part 1 — With Desmos (10 questions · every one is faster on the graph)

The SAT gives you Desmos on every maths question. Here it is a fraction calculator. Type the numerator and denominator you have chosen — the whole difficulty of this topic is choosing the denominator, and Desmos cannot do that.

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. One question decides almost all of these: has the group been narrowed? If the wording says ‘given that’, ‘of the’ or ‘among’, the denominator is a row or a column, not the whole table.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
The table shows the results of a survey of 180 market customers. If one customer is selected at random, what is the probability that the customer bought cheese?
4/9

The Cheese column totals 60 + 20 = 80, out of the grand total 180.

80/180 = 4/9. A common wrong answer is the single overlap cell 60/180.

P2Hard
Using the same table: of the customers who bought fruit, what is the probability that the customer also bought cheese?
3/5

‘Of the customers who bought fruit’ makes the Fruit row, 100, the whole.

60/100 = 3/5. A common wrong answer divides by 180 instead — the single most common error on this topic.

P3Hard
A bag contains 5 red, 4 blue and 3 green counters. One counter is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is not green?
3/4

Not green means 5 + 4 = 9 of the 12 counters.

9/12 = 3/4. A common wrong answer is P(green) itself.

P4Hard
A bag contains 5 red and 3 blue counters. Two counters are drawn at random without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
5/14

First draw 5/8; after one red is removed, 4 reds remain of 7.

(5/8)(4/7) = 20/56 = 5/14. A common wrong answer is the answer if the counter is replaced.

P5Hard
A card is drawn at random from a standard deck of 52. What is the probability that it is a heart or a king?
4/13

13 hearts + 4 kings, minus the king of hearts counted twice.

(13 + 4 − 1)/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. Forgetting to subtract gives 17/52.

P6Hard
The probability that a customer at a market buys cheese is 4/9. On a day when 450 customers visit, how many would be expected to buy cheese?
200

Expected count = probability × group size.

(4/9)(450) = 200 customers.

P7Very
hard
Using the survey table, what is the probability that a randomly chosen customer bought fruit or cheese?
2/3

100/180 + 80/180 would double-count the 60 who did both.

(100 + 80 − 60)/180 = 120/180 = 2/3. A common wrong answer is what you get by adding 100 and 80 and not subtracting the overlap.

P8Very
hard
In the same survey, let A be ‘bought cheese given bought fruit’ and B be ‘bought fruit given bought cheese’. State what is true here.
A < B, because 100 is larger than 80.

A = 60/100 = 0.6 and B = 60/80 = 0.75, so A < B.

The numerator is the same 60 both times; only the denominator changes, and the larger denominator gives the smaller probability. A common wrong answer is the classic error of treating conditional probability as symmetric.

P9Very
hard
A quality check finds that 3% of parts are faulty. In a batch of 1,200 parts, two are drawn at random with replacement. What is the probability that both are faulty?
0.0009

With replacement the draws are independent.

(0.03)(0.03) = 0.0009. A common wrong answer adds the two probabilities instead of multiplying; the batch size of 1,200 is not needed at all.

P10Very
hard
A spinner has 8 equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. It is spun twice. What is the probability that both spins give a number greater than 5?
9/64

Each spin: 6, 7, 8 qualify, so 3/8. The spins are independent.

(3/8)(3/8) = 9/64. A common wrong answer is one spin only.

P11Very
hard
In a survey of 180 customers, 100 bought fruit and 60 of those also bought cheese; 20 of the remaining 80 bought cheese. A manager claims that buying fruit and buying cheese are independent. Which calculation best tests the claim?
Compare 60/100 with 80/180.

Independence means P(cheese | fruit) equals P(cheese).

P(cheese | fruit) = 60/100 = 0.6 and P(cheese) = 80/180 ≈ 0.44. They differ, so the events are not independent and the claim fails. A common wrong answer compares the two conditional probabilities, which tests something else.

P12Very
hard
Of 100 fruit buyers surveyed, 60 also bought cheese. A town has 2,500 fruit buyers. Assuming the same rate, how many are expected to buy cheese?
1500

The rate is 60/100 = 0.6.

0.6 × 2500 = 1,500 people.

The one habit to build. Your class scored 20% on conditional probability, and the cause is always the same: the right numerator over the wrong denominator. Before dividing, say which group you are now inside.

SAT Math 3.7 — Inference & Margin of Error

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Population, sample and parameter

the population is everyone you want to describe | the sample is who you actually asked

A statistic comes from the sample; a parameter describes the population. The whole point of sampling is to estimate the parameter you cannot measure. The sample must be drawn from the population you want to describe — surveying one school tells you nothing about a country.

Example 1. A school of 1,200 students is surveyed by asking 150 of them. Name the population and the sample.
Solution.

Population = the 1,200 students; sample = the 150 asked.

Example 2. In that survey 60% of those asked walk to school. Is 60% a statistic or a parameter?
Solution.

It comes from the sample, so it is a statistic.

It estimates the unknown parameter, the true percentage among all 1,200.

Example 3. A researcher wants to describe all adults in a city but surveys only gym members. What is wrong?
Solution.

The sample is not drawn from the whole population, so it is biased.

Gym members differ systematically from adults in general, and no sample size fixes that.

2Random selection and bias

only a random sample supports generalising to the population

Bias is about how people were chosen, not how many. A voluntary online poll, a convenience sample at one location, or a survey of people who chose to reply are all biased no matter how large. Increasing a biased sample makes the wrong answer more precise, not more correct.

Example 1. A survey is posted online and 5,000 people reply voluntarily. Is it reliable for the population?
Solution.

No. Voluntary response is biased — people with strong opinions answer.

5,000 replies do not repair that.

Example 2. Which is better for estimating a school's average: 60 randomly chosen students, or 300 volunteers?
Solution.

The 60 random students. Random selection removes systematic bias; volunteering does not.

Example 3. A council surveys shoppers at one shopping centre on a Tuesday morning. Name the problem.
Solution.

A convenience sample. Tuesday-morning shoppers are not representative of all residents, so the results cannot be generalised.

3Margin of error

plausible interval = estimate ± margin of error

The margin of error turns a single estimate into a range of believable values for the population. The SAT never asks you to compute one from scratch; it asks you to build the interval, read it, or say what changes it.

Example 1. A poll estimates 62% with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Give the plausible interval.
Solution.

62 − 4 = 58 and 62 + 4 = 66.

The interval is 58% to 66%.

Example 2. Is a true value of 57% consistent with that poll?
Solution.

No. 57% lies outside 58%–66%, so it is not among the plausible values.

Example 3. A second poll reports 62% with a margin of error of 1.5 points. What is its interval?
Solution.

60.5% to 63.5% — a narrower, more precise estimate of the same quantity.

4What makes the margin of error smaller

a larger sample narrows it | a higher confidence level widens it

Sample size is the lever the SAT tests. More data gives a tighter interval, but with diminishing returns — the margin shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so quadrupling the sample roughly halves it. Population size is almost irrelevant.

Example 1. A survey of 400 gives a margin of error of 5 points. What would 1,600 give, roughly?
Solution.

Four times the sample roughly halves the margin.

About 2.5 points.

Example 2. Two polls of the same population report margins of 2 and 6 points. Which used a larger sample?
Solution.

The one with the 2-point margin — smaller margin, larger sample.

Example 3. Does raising the confidence level from 95% to 99% make the interval wider or narrower?
Solution.

Wider. To be more confident of capturing the true value, you must allow a bigger range.

5Reading a confidence statement

the interval is about the population value, not about individuals

The language matters more than the arithmetic. A 95% confidence interval of 58% to 66% says the plausible values for the whole population lie in that range. It does not say 95% of people, and it does not say any individual has a 95% chance of anything.

Example 1. A poll gives a 95% confidence interval of 58% to 66% for the share who walk to school. State what it means.
Solution.

It is plausible that the true percentage for the whole population lies between 58% and 66%.

Example 2. Does it mean 95% of students walk to school?
Solution.

No. 95% is the confidence level, not a percentage of students.

The estimate of walkers is 62%.

Example 3. Two groups' intervals are 58–66% and 64–72%. Can you say one group is higher?
Solution.

Not confidently — the intervals overlap between 64% and 66%, so the same true value is plausible for both.

6Which conclusions a study supports

random selection → generalise | random assignment → cause

Two different randomisations license two different conclusions, and the SAT keeps them apart. Selecting participants at random lets you extend findings to the population. Assigning them to groups at random lets you claim the treatment caused the difference. You need both for both.

Example 1. 200 students are chosen at random from a school and surveyed. What can you conclude?
Solution.

You may generalise to that school, but not to other schools and not about cause.

Example 2. Volunteers are randomly assigned to two study methods and one scores higher. What follows?
Solution.

You may claim the method caused the difference for people like these volunteers, but you cannot generalise beyond them.

Example 3. A study randomly selects participants from a city and randomly assigns them to treatments. What is supported?
Solution.

Both a causal claim and generalisation to that city — the strongest design the SAT will show you.

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Two questions answer nearly all of these: who was sampled, and is the claimed value inside the interval. Neither needs a calculation.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
A researcher surveys 150 students selected at random from the 1,200 students at a school and finds that 60% walk to school. Which is the parameter of interest?
The percentage of all 1,200 students who walk to school.

A parameter describes the population. The 60% is a statistic that estimates it.

The groups in B and D are the sample and the population themselves, not percentages.

P2Hard
A poll of registered voters estimates that 62% support a proposal, with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which interval gives the plausible values for the whole population?
58% to 66%

Estimate ± margin of error: 62 − 4 to 62 + 4.

58% to 66%. Two common wrong answers use the margin on one side only.

P3Hard
A website posts a survey and 5,000 readers choose to respond. Which is the strongest objection to generalising the results to all adults in the country?
Respondents chose themselves, so the sample is biased.

This is voluntary response bias: people with strong views reply.

5,000 is a large sample, so A is wrong — and a large biased sample is still biased.

P4Hard
A survey of 400 people produces a margin of error of 5 percentage points. Approximately what margin of error would a survey of 1,600 similar people produce?
2.5

The margin shrinks with the square root of the sample size, so four times the sample roughly halves it.

About 2.5 points. A common wrong answer divides by 4 instead of by 2.

P5Hard
A 95% confidence interval for the percentage of residents who recycle runs from 58% to 66%. What is the margin of error, in percentage points?
4

The interval is the estimate ± the margin, so the margin is half its width.

(66 − 58)/2 = 4 percentage points.

P6Hard
In a town of 24,000 adults, a random sample estimates that 38% support a new library. Approximately how many adults in the town does this estimate represent?
9120

0.38 × 24,000 = 9,120 adults.

P7Very
hard
A study reports a 95% confidence interval of 58% to 66% for the share of students who walk to school. State the best-supported conclusion.
It is plausible that the true percentage for all students is between 58% and 66%.

The interval describes plausible values for the population percentage.

A common wrong answer confuses the confidence level with the quantity measured; B treats an estimate as exact.

P8Very
hard
Two schools are surveyed. School A's interval for the proportion who walk is 58% to 66%; School B's is 64% to 72%. What can be concluded?
The intervals overlap, so the data does not establish which school is higher.

The intervals share the range 64%–66%, so a single true value could sit in both.

No confident difference can be claimed. Overlap is the thing to look for.

P9Very
hard
Researchers randomly select 200 adults from a city and randomly assign them to one of two exercise programmes. Programme A's group shows greater improvement. State the best-supported conclusion.
Programme A causes greater improvement for adults in that city.

Random assignment supports the causal claim; random selection from the city supports generalising to that city — but no further.

A common wrong answer over-reaches to a population never sampled.

P10Very
hard
A council wants to estimate the average commute time of all its residents. It surveys shoppers at one shopping centre on a Tuesday morning. Which change would most improve the study?
Select residents at random from the council's records.

The flaw is how people were chosen, not how many.

Only random selection from the whole population removes it; A makes a biased estimate more precise, not more accurate.

P11Very
hard
A poll of 1,000 people reports 45% support with a margin of error of 3 points. The pollster then reports 45% with a margin of error of 3 points for a subgroup of only 100 of those people. What is wrong?
The subgroup is ten times smaller, so its margin of error must be larger — roughly 9.5 points.

Margin of error depends on sample size. A tenth of the sample widens the margin by a factor of about √10 ≈ 3.2, so roughly 3 × 3.2 ≈ 9.5 points.

Reusing the full-sample margin for a subgroup overstates the precision badly.

P12Very
hard
A survey of a random sample of 150 of a school's 1,200 students finds 90 walk to school, with a margin of error of 7 percentage points. What is the lower end of the plausible interval for the whole school, as a percentage?
53

The sample estimate is 90/150 = 60%.

60 − 7 = 53%. The population size of 1,200 plays no part in the calculation.

The one habit to build. A margin of error covers sampling variation and nothing else. It does not cover a biased sample, a leading question or people answering dishonestly — and no sample size will fix those.

SAT Math 3.8 — Evaluating Statistical Claims

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Observational study or experiment?

a study that only watches cannot show cause | an experiment imposes a treatment

Ask one question: did the researchers decide who got what? If they merely recorded what people already did, it is observational and the strongest claim available is association. If they assigned the treatment, it is an experiment and cause is on the table.

Example 1. Researchers record the diets of 500 adults and their blood pressure. Which type of study is this?
Solution.

Observational. Nobody was told what to eat, so no causal claim is supported.

Example 2. Researchers randomly give 250 adults diet A and 250 diet B, then measure blood pressure. Which type?
Solution.

An experiment — the treatment was imposed, and at random.

Example 3. Why can the first study not show that diet causes high blood pressure?
Solution.

People who choose a diet differ in other ways too — age, income, exercise.

Any of these confounding variables could explain the difference.

2Random selection versus random assignment

random selection → generalise to the population | random assignment → claim cause

These two are constantly swapped on the SAT. Selection is how people entered the study; assignment is how they were split once inside. Each buys exactly one conclusion, and you need both to get both.

Example 1. Volunteers are randomly assigned to two tutoring methods. What can and cannot be concluded?
Solution.

Can: the method caused the difference, for people like these volunteers.

Cannot: generalise to all students — the volunteers were not randomly selected.

Example 2. A random sample of a city's residents is surveyed about commuting. What is supported?
Solution.

Generalisation to that city's residents. No treatment was imposed, so no causal claim.

Example 3. Which design supports both conclusions?
Solution.

Random selection from the population and random assignment to groups — a randomised experiment on a random sample.

3Confounding variables

a third variable linked to both the cause and the effect

When a question asks why an observational result may mislead, the answer is usually a named third variable. A good answer identifies something plausibly connected to both quantities — not just any difference between the groups.

Example 1. Towns with more parks have lower obesity rates. Suggest a confounding variable.
Solution.

Household income. Wealthier areas tend to have both more parks and lower obesity, so the parks may not be the cause.

Example 2. Children with larger shoe sizes read better. What explains it?
Solution.

Age. Older children have bigger feet and read better; shoe size causes nothing.

Example 3. Why does random assignment remove confounding?
Solution.

It spreads the other variables evenly across the groups on average, so the groups differ only in the treatment.

4How the sample limits the conclusion

you may generalise only to the population the sample was drawn from

Match the conclusion to the sampling frame. A random sample of one school supports claims about that school and nothing wider. The commonest wrong answer on these questions is a true-sounding statement about a population that was never sampled.

Example 1. 200 students are chosen at random from one school. To whom do the results apply?
Solution.

To that school's students only — not to the district, and not to students generally.

Example 2. A study samples randomly from all adults in one city. A newspaper reports the result as a national finding. What is wrong?
Solution.

The sampling frame was one city, so the conclusion cannot be stretched to the country.

Example 3. A sample is drawn at random from members of a sports club. Can the result describe the town?
Solution.

No. The population is the club's members; club members differ systematically from the town as a whole.

5Judging a reported claim

check three things: how chosen, how assigned, how far stretched

Most of these questions give you a headline and four conclusions, and the right one is the cautious one. Scan for the overreach: a causal verb on an observational study, or a population wider than the one sampled.

Example 1. Headline: ‘Students who eat breakfast score higher — so schools should serve breakfast.’ Evaluate it.
Solution.

The data is observational, so it shows association only.

Families who provide breakfast may differ in other ways. The recommendation outruns the evidence.

Example 2. A randomised trial on 300 volunteers finds a drug works. A report says it works for everyone. What is the flaw?
Solution.

Random assignment supports cause within the trial, but the volunteers were not randomly selected, so the result cannot be generalised to everyone.

Example 3. What one change would let the breakfast study support its recommendation?
Solution.

Randomly assign students to receive breakfast or not, then compare — turning the observational study into an experiment.

6Precision, bias and sample size

a bigger sample narrows the margin of error | only better selection removes bias

Sample size and bias solve different problems and the SAT tests whether you know which. A larger sample makes the estimate more precise; it does nothing about a sample drawn from the wrong people.

Example 1. A biased survey of 500 is repeated with 5,000 people the same way. What improves?
Solution.

Precision only. The margin of error narrows, but the estimate is still centred on the wrong value.

Example 2. A survey of 400 gives a margin of 5 points. What does 1,600 give, roughly?
Solution.

About 2.5 points — four times the sample roughly halves the margin.

Example 3. Which fixes bias: a larger sample, or random selection?
Solution.

Random selection. Size addresses precision; selection addresses bias, and no amount of size repairs bad selection.

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Run the two-question test on every one: was selection random? (how far it generalises) and was assignment random? (whether cause may be claimed). They are independent.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
Researchers recorded the diets and blood pressure of 500 adults who had each chosen their own diet, and found that a high-salt diet was associated with higher blood pressure. State the best-supported conclusion.
There is an association between the two, but the study cannot establish cause.

Nobody was assigned a diet, so this is an observational study and only association follows.

Two common wrong answers assert a direction of cause the design cannot support.

P2Hard
In a study, 300 volunteers are randomly assigned to either a new tutoring method or the usual one, and the new method's group scores higher. State the best-supported conclusion.
The new method causes higher scores for people like these volunteers.

Random assignment supports a causal claim, but the volunteers were not randomly selected, so the finding cannot be stretched beyond people like them.

A common wrong answer is the classic overreach.

P3Hard
A study finds that towns with more public parks have lower obesity rates. Which is the most plausible confounding variable?
The average household income of the town.

A confounder must plausibly affect both quantities. Wealthier towns tend to have more parks and lower obesity.

Two common wrong answers name the two variables already in the study.

P4Hard
A researcher randomly selects 200 students from one school and surveys them about study habits. To which group may the results be generalised?
All students at that school.

The sample was drawn at random from that school, so the conclusion extends to that school and no further.

A common wrong answer is too cautious: random sampling is exactly what licenses the step from sample to school.

P5Hard
A survey of 400 people reports a margin of error of 5 percentage points. The researchers repeat it with 1,600 people, sampled the same biased way. Which improves?
Precision only; the estimate is still centred on the wrong value.

A larger sample narrows the margin of error, so the estimate becomes more precise.

But the same flawed selection means it is still precisely wrong. Size does not fix bias.

P6Very
hard
Two studies are described. Study 1 randomly selects 500 adults from a city and surveys their exercise habits. Study 2 takes 500 volunteers and randomly assigns them to two exercise programmes. State the best-supported conclusion.
Study 1 supports generalisation to the city; Study 2 supports a causal claim for its participants.

Random selection (Study 1) buys generalisation; random assignment (Study 2) buys cause.

A common wrong answer swaps them, which is the error the question is built around.

P7Very
hard
A newspaper reports: ‘Students who eat breakfast score higher on tests, so schools should provide breakfast.’ The data came from a survey of students' existing habits. What is the main flaw?
The recommendation assumes cause from an observational study.

The survey recorded what students already did, so it shows association only. Families who provide breakfast may differ in other ways.

The recommendation needs an experiment behind it.

P8Very
hard
A clinical trial randomly assigns 300 patients, all recruited from one hospital, to a drug or a placebo. The drug group improves significantly more. State the best-supported conclusion.
The drug caused the improvement in this group of patients.

Random assignment establishes cause within the trial.

Recruitment from a single hospital is not random selection from any wider population, so A over-reaches; C under-reads the assignment.

P9Very
hard
A researcher wants to estimate the average commute time of all adults in a city and surveys every adult leaving one train station at 8 a.m. Which single change would most improve the study?
Select adults at random from the city's electoral register.

The flaw is the sampling frame: train users are not all adults, and no sample size fixes that.

Only random selection from the whole population does. A common wrong answer makes a biased estimate more precise, not more accurate.

P10Very
hard
In an experiment, 250 adults on diet A improved by a mean of 6.4 units and 250 on diet B by a mean of 4.1 units. Assignment was random. What is the difference in mean improvement?
2.3

6.4 − 4.1 = 2.3 units.

Because assignment was random, this difference can reasonably be attributed to the diets.

P11Very
hard
A town has 24,000 adults. A random sample estimates 38% support for a proposal, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Approximately how many adults does the lower end of the plausible interval represent?
8400

Lower end = 38 − 3 = 35%.

0.35 × 24,000 = 8,400 adults.

P12Very
hard
Of 500 adults in an observational study, 180 reported a high-salt diet. What percentage of the sample is this?
36

180/500 = 0.36 = 36%.

Note this is a statistic about the sample; extending it to the population needs the sample to have been randomly selected.

The one habit to build. Selection and assignment are two different things and answer two different questions. Most wrong answers on this topic are true statements about the wrong group, or causal claims from data where nobody assigned anything.

SAT Math 4.1 — Lines, Angles & Triangles

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Angles on a line and at a point

straight line = 180° | full turn = 360° | vertical angles are equal

Complementary angles add to 90°; supplementary to 180°. Vertical (opposite) angles made by two crossing lines are always equal. Most angle-chasing questions are one of these three facts applied twice.

Example 1. Two angles are complementary. One is 3x° and the other (2x + 10)°. Find x.
Solution.

3x + 2x + 10 = 90, so 5x = 80.

x = 16.

Example 2. Two angles on a straight line are (4x)° and (x + 30)°. Find x.
Solution.

4x + x + 30 = 180, so 5x = 150.

x = 30.

Example 3. Two lines cross. One angle is 65°. Find the other three.
Solution.

The vertical angle is 65°; the two adjacent ones are each 180 − 65 = 115°.

2Parallel lines and a transversal

corresponding and alternate angles are equal | co-interior angles add to 180°

When a line crosses two parallels, every angle is either equal to a given one or supplementary to it. Find the equal pairs first; everything else follows from 180°.

Example 1. Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal and one angle is 72°. What is its corresponding angle?
Solution.

Corresponding angles are equal.

72°.

Example 2. What is the co-interior angle to that 72°?
Solution.

Co-interior angles add to 180°.

180 − 72 = 108°.

Example 3. In the figure above, angles 4 and 5 are what kind of pair?
Solution.

They sit between the parallels on opposite sides of the transversal: alternate interior, so they are equal.

3Triangle angle facts

angles sum to 180° | an exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles

The exterior-angle shortcut saves a step: instead of finding the third angle and subtracting from 180, add the two far angles directly.

Example 1. A triangle has angles 50° and 60°. Find the third.
Solution.

180 − 50 − 60 = 70°.

Example 2. For that triangle, what is the exterior angle at the 60° vertex?
Solution.

It equals the two remote interior angles: 50 + 70 = 120°. Checking: 180 − 60 = 120.

Example 3. A triangle’s angles are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. Find the largest.
Solution.

The parts total 9, and 180/9 = 20° per part.

The largest is 4 × 20 = 80°.

4Isosceles and equilateral triangles

equal sides face equal angles | equilateral → every angle 60°

The tick marks on a diagram are doing real work: two marked sides mean two equal base angles. This turns most isosceles questions into a single equation.

Example 1. An isosceles triangle has apex angle 40°. Find each base angle.
Solution.

The two base angles are equal: (180 − 40)/2.

70° each.

Example 2. An isosceles triangle has a base angle of 50°. Find the apex angle.
Solution.

Both base angles are 50°.

180 − 100 = 80°.

Example 3. Why can an isosceles triangle not have two angles of 100°?
Solution.

They would total 200°, already above 180°. The equal angles in an isosceles triangle must each be below 90°.

5The triangle inequality

any two sides must add to more than the third

Given two sides a and b, the third side x satisfies |a − b| < x < a + b. Questions ask for the possible values, or for the largest or smallest whole number that works.

Example 1. Two sides are 7 and 10. What values can the third side take?
Solution.

10 − 7 < x < 10 + 7.

3 < x < 17.

Example 2. For those sides, what is the largest possible whole-number third side?
Solution.

x must be below 17.

16.

Example 3. Can a triangle have sides 4, 5 and 9?
Solution.

4 + 5 = 9, which is not more than 9.

No — it collapses flat.

6Polygons and quadrilaterals

interior angles of an n-gon sum to (n − 2) × 180° | exterior angles always sum to 360°

The exterior-angle fact is the quicker route for regular polygons: each exterior angle is 360/n, and the interior angle is its supplement. In a parallelogram opposite angles are equal and adjacent ones add to 180°.

Example 1. Find the sum of the interior angles of a hexagon.
Solution.

(6 − 2) × 180 = 720°.

Example 2. Find each interior angle of a regular hexagon.
Solution.

Each exterior angle is 360/6 = 60°.

Interior = 180 − 60 = 120°.

Example 3. A regular polygon has interior angles of 150°. How many sides?
Solution.

Each exterior angle is 30°, and they total 360°.

360/30 = 12 sides.

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Mark every angle you can deduce on the figure before you write an equation. Most of these fall out in two steps once the diagram is labelled.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
Two angles are complementary. One angle measures 3x° and the other measures (2x + 10)°. What is the value of x?
16

Complementary means they total 90°: 3x + 2x + 10 = 90, so 5x = 80.

x = 16. Using 180 instead of 90 gives 34, which is not an option — a useful check.

P2Hard
In the figure, two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. If angle 1 measures 72°, what is the measure of angle 3, in degrees?
108

Angles 1 and 3 sit on a straight line, so they are supplementary.

180 − 72 = 108°.

P3Hard
In a triangle, two of the angles measure 50° and 60°. What is the measure of the exterior angle at the third vertex, in degrees?
110

The third interior angle is 180 − 110 = 70°, and its exterior angle is 180 − 70 = 110°.

Equivalently, the exterior angle equals the two remote interior angles: 50 + 60 = 110.

P4Hard
An isosceles triangle has an apex angle of 40°. What is the measure of each base angle?
70°

The two base angles are equal and the three total 180°.

(180 − 40)/2 = 70°. A common wrong answer is the sum of the two base angles, not each one.

P5Hard
The angles of a triangle are in the ratio 2 : 3 : 4. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
80

The ratio has 2 + 3 + 4 = 9 parts, and 180/9 = 20° per part.

4 × 20 = 80°.

P6Hard
Two sides of a triangle measure 7 and 10. State the range of possible lengths for the third side.
3 < x < 17

The third side x must satisfy 3 < x < 17.

Both boundaries are excluded, and each would give a flat, degenerate triangle.

P7Very
hard
In a regular polygon, each interior angle measures 150°. How many sides does the polygon have?
12

Each exterior angle is 180 − 150 = 30°, and the exterior angles always total 360°.

360/30 = 12 sides.

P8Very
hard
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One of the eight angles formed measures (3x + 10)° and the co-interior angle on the same side measures (2x − 5)°. What is the value of x?
35

Co-interior angles are supplementary: 3x + 10 + 2x − 5 = 180, so 5x + 5 = 180.

x = 35. Setting them equal instead gives x = −15, which is impossible — a sign you chose the wrong angle relationship.

P9Very
hard
In triangle ABC, angle A measures (2x)°, angle B measures (3x + 10)°, and angle C measures (x + 20)°. What is the measure of the largest angle, in degrees?
85°

2x + 3x + 10 + x + 20 = 180 gives 6x + 30 = 180, so x = 25.

The angles are 50°, 85° and 45°, so the largest is 85°. A common wrong answer is x itself, which is not an angle of the triangle.

P10Very
hard
A parallelogram has one angle measuring 65°. What is the measure of the angle adjacent to it, in degrees?
115

Adjacent angles of a parallelogram are supplementary.

180 − 65 = 115°. The opposite angle, by contrast, is also 65°.

P11Very
hard
The sum of the interior angles of a polygon is 1,260°. How many sides does it have?
9

(n − 2) × 180 = 1260, so n − 2 = 7.

n = 9. A common wrong answer is n − 2, stopped one step early.

P12Very
hard
In the figure, two lines intersect and one of the four angles formed measures (5x − 20)°. Its vertical angle measures (3x + 10)°. What is the measure of each of these angles, in degrees?
55°

Vertical angles are equal: 5x − 20 = 3x + 10, so 2x = 30 and x = 15.

The angle is 5(15) − 20 = 55°. A common wrong answer is x itself, not the angle — read what the question asks for.

The one habit to build. Read what the question asks for. Several of these solve to a value of x that is not the answer — the angle is 5x − 20, not x.

SAT Math 4.2 — Similarity & Congruence

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1When are two triangles similar?

AA — two pairs of equal angles is enough | similar means same shape, different size

You never need all three angles: if two match, the third must. Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides, and the SAT almost always gives you the angles and asks for a side.

Example 1. Two triangles have angles 40°, 60° and 40°, 80°. Are they similar?
Solution.

The first has third angle 80°, the second 60°. Both are 40, 60, 80.

Yes, by AA.

Example 2. Two right triangles each have an angle of 35°. Are they similar?
Solution.

Both have 90° and 35°, so the third is 55° in each.

Yes, by AA.

Example 3. Two triangles have sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 11. Are they similar?
Solution.

6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2, but 11/5 = 2.2.

No — the ratios must all match.

2The scale factor

scale factor k = new ÷ old | every matching length multiplies by k

Find k from the one pair of sides you are given, then apply it to the side you want. Pair the sides correctly: the side opposite the 30° angle in one triangle matches the side opposite the 30° angle in the other.

Example 1. A triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is enlarged so the shortest side becomes 9. Find the scale factor.
Solution.

k = 9/3 = 3.

Example 2. For that enlargement, what is the new longest side?
Solution.

5 × 3 = 15.

Example 3. Triangle ABC has AB = 6; similar triangle DEF has DE = 15. If BC = 8, find EF.
Solution.

k = 15/6 = 2.5.

EF = 8 × 2.5 = 20.

3Area and volume scale differently

lengths × k | areas × k² | volumes × k³

This is the trap the SAT returns to. Doubling every length multiplies the area by 4 and the volume by 8. Going the other way, if areas are in the ratio 9 : 4, the lengths are in the ratio 3 : 2 — take the square root.

Example 1. Two similar rectangles have sides in the ratio 2 : 5. What is the ratio of their areas?
Solution.

Square the factor.

4 : 25.

Example 2. Two similar solids have volumes 8 cm³ and 216 cm³. Find the ratio of their heights.
Solution.

216/8 = 27, and the cube root of 27 is 3.

1 : 3.

Example 3. A model is built to scale 1 : 30. The model holds 2 litres. How much does the real tank hold?
Solution.

Volume scales by 30³ = 27,000.

2 × 27,000 = 54,000 litres.

4Similar triangles hidden in one figure

a line parallel to one side cuts off a similar triangle

When a figure contains a line parallel to a side, two similar triangles are sitting inside it. Redraw them separately, the same way round, before writing any ratio.

Example 1. In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC with AD = 4, DB = 6 and AE = 6. Find EC.
Solution.

AD/DB = AE/EC, so 4/6 = 6/EC.

EC = 9.

Example 2. Why are the two triangles similar?
Solution.

DE parallel to BC makes the corresponding angles equal, so AA applies.

Example 3. In that figure, AB = 10 and AC = 15. What is the scale factor from ADE to ABC?
Solution.

AD/AB = 4/10.

k = 2.5 going from the small triangle to the large one.

5Shadows, mirrors and indirect measurement

same sun angle → similar triangles → height/shadow is the same ratio for both

The classic SAT word problem. Write the ratio the same way round for both objects: height ÷ shadow for one equals height ÷ shadow for the other.

Example 1. A 6-foot pole casts a 4-foot shadow. A signpost casts an 18-foot shadow. Find its height.
Solution.

6/4 = h/18, so h = 18 × 1.5 = 27 feet.

Example 2. A 1.8 m person casts a 1.2 m shadow. A tree’s shadow is 8 m. Find the tree’s height.
Solution.

1.8/1.2 = 1.5, and 8 × 1.5 = 12 m.

Example 3. Why must the two shadows be measured at the same time?
Solution.

The sun’s angle changes through the day. Only at the same moment are the two triangles similar.

6Congruence

congruent = same shape and same size, so the scale factor is 1

Congruent triangles match exactly: SSS, SAS, ASA or AAS. Note that AAA gives similarity only, never congruence, because the sizes can differ.

Example 1. Two triangles have all three pairs of sides equal. Are they congruent?
Solution.

Yes, by SSS.

Example 2. Two triangles have all three pairs of angles equal. Are they congruent?
Solution.

Not necessarily — they are similar, but one could be an enlargement of the other.

Example 3. Triangles ABC and DEF are congruent with AB = 7. What is DE?
Solution.

Congruent means the scale factor is 1.

DE = 7.

The SAT gives you Desmos on every maths question. Here it is a proportion solver. Type the ratio as an equation with the unknown in it and read the answer straight off.

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. For every question, first ask whether the quantity being scaled is a length, an area or a volume. That one decision picks the exponent.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
Beside a market stall, a vertical pole 6 feet tall casts a shadow 4 feet long. At the same time of day, a signpost casts a shadow 18 feet long. What is the height of the signpost, in feet?
27

The sun’s angle is the same, so the triangles are similar: 6/4 = h/18.

h = 18 × 1.5 = 27 feet. A common wrong answer comes from 18 − 6, not a ratio at all.

P2Hard
Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF, with AB = 6 and DE = 15. If BC = 8, what is the length of EF?
20

The scale factor is 15/6 = 2.5, and it applies to every pair of matching sides.

EF = 8 × 2.5 = 20.

P3Hard
Two similar rectangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 2 : 5. What is the ratio of their areas?
4 : 25

Area scales by the square of the length ratio.

2² : 5² = 4 : 25. A common wrong answer forgets to square; D cubes it, which is the volume rule for solids.

P4Hard
In triangle ABC, point D lies on AB and point E lies on AC so that DE is parallel to BC. If AD = 4, DB = 6 and AE = 6, what is the length of EC?
9

DE parallel to BC makes the two triangles similar, so AD/DB = AE/EC.

4/6 = 6/EC gives EC = 36/4 = 9.

P5Hard
Two triangles have angles of 40° and 60° in the first, and 40° and 80° in the second. State what is true here.
They are similar, because two angles of each match.

The first triangle’s third angle is 80° and the second’s is 60°, so both have angles 40, 60 and 80.

Similar by AA. Congruence would need the sizes to match too, which nothing here establishes.

P6Hard
A model of a water tank is built to a scale of 1 : 30. The model holds 2 litres. How many litres does the real tank hold?
54,000

Volume scales by the cube of the length factor: 30³ = 27,000.

2 × 27,000 = 54,000 litres. A common wrong answer multiplies by 30 once; B squares it.

P7Very
hard
Two similar solid figures have volumes of 8 cubic centimetres and 216 cubic centimetres. What is the ratio of their corresponding heights?
1 : 3

216/8 = 27, and the height ratio is the cube root of the volume ratio.

∛27 = 3, so the ratio is 1 : 3. A common wrong answer uses the volume ratio itself.

P8Very
hard
Two similar triangles have areas of 9 and 25 square units. The shorter triangle has a side of length 6. What is the length of the corresponding side in the larger triangle?
10

The side ratio is the square root of the area ratio: √(25/9) = 5/3.

6 × 5/3 = 10.

P9Very
hard
Triangles ABC and DEF have all three pairs of angles equal. Which conclusion is guaranteed?
The triangles are similar.

Equal angles guarantee the same shape but say nothing about size.

Similar, and possibly congruent, but AAA alone never proves congruence — one could be an enlargement of the other.

P10Very
hard
A rectangular photograph measuring 4 cm by 6 cm is enlarged by a scale factor of 2.5. What is the area of the enlarged photograph, in square centimetres?
150

Original area 24 cm²; area scales by 2.5² = 6.25.

24 × 6.25 = 150. A common wrong answer multiplies the area by 2.5 once, the commonest error here.

P11Very
hard
Two triangles have sides 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 11 respectively. Are they similar, and why?
No, because the three ratios are not all equal.

6/3 = 2 and 8/4 = 2, but 11/5 = 2.2.

Similarity needs all matching ratios to agree, so they are not similar. A common wrong answer is true but irrelevant — similar triangles normally do have different perimeters.

P12Very
hard
In a figure, triangle ADE sits inside triangle ABC with DE parallel to BC. AD = 4, AB = 10 and the area of triangle ADE is 12 square units. What is the area of triangle ABC, in square units?
75

The length factor is AB/AD = 10/4 = 2.5, so the area factor is 2.5² = 6.25.

12 × 6.25 = 75. A common wrong answer applies the length factor 2.5 to the area directly instead of squaring it.

The one habit to build. Areas scale by k squared and volumes by k cubed. Your class scored 47% here, and almost every lost mark was a length factor applied to an area or a volume.

SAT Math 4.3 — Right Triangles & Trigonometry

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Pythagoras

a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse — the side opposite the right angle

Identify the hypotenuse before substituting. It is always the longest side and always opposite the right angle. Putting a leg where c belongs is the error that costs this topic its marks.

Example 1. A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Find the hypotenuse.
Solution.

81 + 144 = 225.

c = √225 = 15.

Example 2. A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. Find the other leg.
Solution.

Here 13 is c, so 25 + b² = 169.

b = √144 = 12.

Example 3. A drone flies 9 km east then 12 km north. How far is it from the start?
Solution.

The path makes a right angle.

√(81 + 144) = 15 km.

2The triples worth memorising

3-4-5 | 5-12-13 | 8-15-17 | 7-24-25 — and all their multiples

Recognising a triple turns a calculation into a glance. 9-12-15 is 3-4-5 tripled; 10-24-26 is 5-12-13 doubled. If two sides fit a triple, the third is immediate.

Example 1. A right triangle has legs 9 and 12. Which triple is this?
Solution.

3-4-5 multiplied by 3.

The hypotenuse is 5 × 3 = 15.

Example 2. A right triangle has hypotenuse 26 and one leg 10. Find the other leg.
Solution.

5-12-13 doubled.

The other leg is 12 × 2 = 24.

Example 3. Is a triangle with sides 8, 15, 17 right-angled?
Solution.

64 + 225 = 289 = 17².

Yes — the converse of Pythagoras.

3Special right triangles

45-45-90 → sides 1 : 1 : √2 | 30-60-90 → sides 1 : √3 : 2

These two appear constantly and are on the reference sheet. In a 30-60-90 the shortest side faces the 30° angle and is half the hypotenuse; the √3 side faces the 60°.

Example 1. A 45-45-90 triangle has legs of 5. Find the hypotenuse.
Solution.

5 × √2 = 5√2 ≈ 7.07.

Example 2. A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 10. Find the shortest side.
Solution.

The side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse.

5.

Example 3. For that triangle, find the remaining side.
Solution.

It faces the 60° angle: 5√3 ≈ 8.66.

4SOH-CAH-TOA

sin = opp/hyp | cos = adj/hyp | tan = opp/adj

Label the three sides relative to the angle you are working with before choosing a ratio. Opposite and adjacent swap when you switch angles; the hypotenuse never moves.

Example 1. In a right triangle, sin A = 0.6 and the hypotenuse is 20. Find the side opposite A.
Solution.

sin A = opp/hyp, so opp = 0.6 × 20 = 12.

Example 2. A ramp makes an angle whose sine is 0.6 and is 20 feet long. How high is the top?
Solution.

The ramp is the hypotenuse.

0.6 × 20 = 12 feet.

Example 3. In a right triangle, the side adjacent to angle B is 8 and the hypotenuse is 17. Find cos B.
Solution.

cos B = adj/hyp = 8/17 ≈ 0.471.

5Finding an angle

use inverse trig: if tan θ = 3/4 then θ = tan⁻¹(3/4)

When the sides are known and the angle is not, the inverse functions give it. In Desmos type arctan, arcsin or arccos and make sure the calculator is in degrees.

Example 1. A right triangle has opposite 3 and adjacent 4. Find the angle, to the nearest degree.
Solution.

tan θ = 0.75, so θ = tan⁻¹(0.75) ≈ 37°.

Example 2. A ladder 10 m long reaches 8 m up a wall. What angle does it make with the ground?
Solution.

sin θ = 8/10 = 0.8.

θ = sin⁻¹(0.8) ≈ 53°.

Example 3. Why do those two answers add to about 90°?
Solution.

They are the two acute angles of similar right triangles — 3-4-5 in both cases.

6sin θ = cos(90° − θ)

the sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement

In a right triangle the two acute angles add to 90°, and what is opposite one is adjacent to the other. So sin and cos swap. Questions set sin(expression) = cos(expression) and ask you to make the two angles add to 90.

Example 1. If sin 35° = cos x° and x is acute, find x.
Solution.

x = 90 − 35 = 55.

Example 2. In a right triangle the acute angles are (2x + 10)° and (3x − 20)°. Find x.
Solution.

They are complementary: 2x + 10 + 3x − 20 = 90, so 5x = 100.

x = 20.

Example 3. If sin A = 3/5 for an acute angle A, what is cos(90° − A)?
Solution.

3/5 — it is the same quantity, by the identity.

Part 1 — With Desmos (10 questions · draw the figure; the picture is faster than the algebra)

The SAT gives you Desmos on every maths question. Here it is a trig calculator. Use arcsin, arccos and arctan for angles, and check the setting is degrees before you trust anything.

D3A 45-45-90 triangle has legs of 5. What is the hypotenuse, to two decimal places?5*sqrt(2)Desmos keeps the exact form too.7.07
D4A 30-60-90 triangle has hypotenuse 10. What is the side opposite 60°, to two decimals?5*sqrt(3)Half the hypotenuse, times √3.8.66

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Label opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the angle in the question before choosing a ratio. Opposite and adjacent swap when the angle does.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
A drone takes off from a stadium, flies 9 kilometres due east, then 12 kilometres due north. What is the straight-line distance, in kilometres, between the drone and the stadium?
15

East and north are perpendicular, so this is a right triangle.

√(81 + 144) = √225 = 15 km. It is 3-4-5 tripled.

P2Hard
A straight loading ramp forms a right triangle with the level ground. The sine of the angle between the ramp and the ground is 0.6, and the ramp is 20 feet long. How many feet above the ground is the top of the ramp?
12

The ramp is the hypotenuse, and sin = opp/hyp.

0.6 × 20 = 12 feet. A common wrong answer divides 20 by 0.6 × 2 or similar — the clue is that the opposite side must be shorter than the hypotenuse.

P3Hard
In right triangle ABC, the right angle is at C and the hypotenuse AB = 13. If BC = 5, what is the length of AC?
12

AB is the hypotenuse, so 5² + AC² = 13².

AC = √144 = 12. This is the 5-12-13 triple.

P4Hard
A 30-60-90 triangle has a hypotenuse of length 10. What is the length of the side opposite the 30° angle?
5

In a 30-60-90 triangle the side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse.

10/2 = 5. A common wrong answer is the side opposite 60°.

P5Hard
If sin 35° = cos x° and 0 < x < 90, what is the value of x?
55

sin θ = cos(90° − θ).

x = 90 − 35 = 55.

P6Hard
A 45-45-90 triangle has legs of length 5. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
5√2

In a 45-45-90 triangle the sides are in the ratio 1 : 1 : √2.

The hypotenuse is 5√2 ≈ 7.07. A common wrong answer doubles the leg instead.

P7Very
hard
In a right-triangle design on a banner, the two acute angles measure (2x + 10)° and (3x − 20)°, so sin((2x + 10)°) = cos((3x − 20)°). What is the value of x?
20

The identity holds exactly when the two angles are complementary.

2x + 10 + 3x − 20 = 90 gives 5x = 100, so x = 20. The angles are 50° and 40°.

P8Very
hard
A ladder 10 metres long leans against a wall and reaches 8 metres up it. What angle, to the nearest degree, does the ladder make with the ground?
53°

The wall height is opposite the angle and the ladder is the hypotenuse: sin θ = 0.8.

θ = sin⁻¹(0.8) ≈ 53°. A common wrong answer is the angle at the top of the ladder, the complement.

P9Very
hard
A right triangle has legs of length 8 and 15. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
17

64 + 225 = 289, and √289 = 17 — the 8-15-17 triple.

A common wrong answer comes from subtracting instead of adding the squares.

P10Very
hard
In right triangle ABC the right angle is at C, and sin A = 3/5. What is the value of cos B?
3/5

Angles A and B are complementary, and sin A = cos(90° − A) = cos B.

cos B = 3/5. A common wrong answer is cos A, which answers a different question.

P11Very
hard
A right triangle has an angle whose tangent is 3/4. If the side adjacent to that angle is 12, what is the length of the hypotenuse?
15

tan = opp/adj = 3/4, so with adj = 12 the opposite is 9.

This is 9-12-15, which is 3-4-5 tripled, so the hypotenuse is 15. A common wrong answer is the opposite side, not the hypotenuse.

P12Very
hard
A rectangular field measures 40 metres by 30 metres. A path runs diagonally from one corner to the opposite corner. How much shorter, in metres, is the diagonal path than walking along two sides?
20

The diagonal is √(1600 + 900) = √2500 = 50 m, and two sides total 70 m.

70 − 50 = 20 metres shorter.

The one habit to build. Find the hypotenuse first and write it down. Your class scored 20% on Pythagoras, and the usual cause is putting a leg where c belongs — the hypotenuse is always opposite the right angle and always the longest side.

SAT Math 4.4 — Circles

Explanations with worked examples · diagrams for every rule · Desmos questions | Teacher copy — with solutions · Grade 11 · Ellipse International School

1Circumference and area

C = 2πr | A = πr² — both are on the reference sheet

Almost every circle question starts by finding r. If you are given the area, take the square root; if the circumference, divide by 2π. Then answer what was asked.

Example 1. A circle has area 64π. Find its circumference.
Solution.

πr² = 64π gives r = 8.

C = 2π(8) = 16π.

Example 2. A circle has circumference 18π. Find its area.
Solution.

2πr = 18π gives r = 9.

A = π(81) = 81π.

Example 3. A circular path encloses 100π square metres. How long is the path?
Solution.

r = 10, so the path is the circumference.

2π(10) = 20π metres.

2Arcs and sectors

arc = (θ/360) × 2πr | sector area = (θ/360) × πr²

A sector is a fraction of the whole circle, and the fraction is the angle over 360. Work out the whole first, then take the slice.

Example 1. A circle of radius 9 has a sector with central angle 80°. Find its area.
Solution.

Whole area = 81π, and 80/360 = 2/9.

(2/9)(81π) = 18π.

Example 2. For that same circle, find the arc length of the sector.
Solution.

Whole circumference = 18π.

(2/9)(18π) = 4π.

Example 3. A sector of a circle of radius 6 has area 6π. Find its central angle.
Solution.

Whole area 36π, and 6π/36π = 1/6.

(1/6)(360) = 60°.

3Central and inscribed angles

a central angle equals its arc | an inscribed angle is half its arc

The vertex position decides the rule: at the centre, the angle equals the arc; on the circle, it is half. The special case worth knowing cold is that an angle inscribed in a semicircle is a right angle.

Example 1. A central angle cuts an arc of 70°. What is the central angle?
Solution.

70° — they are equal.

Example 2. An inscribed angle cuts that same 70° arc. What is the inscribed angle?
Solution.

Half the arc.

35°.

Example 3. Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle with AB a diameter. What is angle ACB?
Solution.

The arc AB is 180°, and the inscribed angle is half.

90°.

4Tangents and chords

a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of contact

A tangent gives you a right angle for free, which usually means Pythagoras is next. A radius drawn perpendicular to a chord also bisects it.

Example 1. A tangent touches a circle of radius 5 at P. From an external point Q, PQ = 12. Find OQ.
Solution.

Angle OPQ is 90°, so OQ² = 25 + 144.

OQ = 13.

Example 2. Why is triangle OPQ right-angled?
Solution.

OP is a radius to the point of contact, and a tangent is perpendicular to the radius there.

Example 3. A chord of length 16 sits in a circle of radius 10. How far is it from the centre?
Solution.

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving legs 8 and d with hypotenuse 10.

d = √(100 − 64) = 6.

5The equation of a circle

(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², centre (h, k), radius r

Read the centre with the signs flipped and remember the right-hand side is r squared, not r. This formula is not on the reference sheet.

Example 1. Find the centre and radius of (x − 3)² + (y + 1)² = 9.
Solution.

Centre (3, −1); radius 3, because 9 = 3².

Example 2. Write the equation of a circle with centre (−2, 5) and radius 4.
Solution.

(x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = 16.

Example 3. Does the point (6, −1) lie on the circle in the first example?
Solution.

(6 − 3)² + (−1 + 1)² = 9 + 0 = 9.

Yes, it is exactly on the circle.

6Completing the square for a circle

group the x terms and the y terms, then halve and square each coefficient

An equation given as x² + y² + Dx + Ey = F has to be rearranged before you can read anything off. Complete the square twice, once for x and once for y.

Example 1. Find the radius of x² + y² − 8x + 6y = 11.
Solution.

(x − 4)² − 16 + (y + 3)² − 9 = 11.

(x − 4)² + (y + 3)² = 36, so r = 6.

Example 2. Find its centre.
Solution.

(4, −3) — the signs flip.

Example 3. Find the radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y = 20.
Solution.

(x + 2)² + (y − 1)² = 20 + 4 + 1 = 25.

r = 5.

Part 1 — With Desmos (10 questions · draw the figure; the picture is faster than the algebra)

The SAT gives you Desmos on every maths question. Here it is a circle grapher. Type the equation in any form and Desmos draws it, centre and radius included — a fast check on your completing the square.

#QuestionType into DesmosThenAnswer
D1A circle has area 64π. What is its circumference as a multiple of π?2*sqrt(64)Radius first, then the circumference.16
D2A circle has circumference 18π. What is its area as a multiple of π?(18/2)^2r = 9, then r squared.81
D3A sector of a circle of radius 9 has central angle 80°. What is its area as a multiple of π?80/360*81Fraction of the whole.18
D4For that same sector, what is the arc length as a multiple of π?80/360*18Same fraction, applied to the circumference.4
D5A sector of a circle of radius 6 has area 6π. What is its central angle in degrees?6/36*360The ratio of areas gives the ratio of angles.60
D6A tangent meets a circle of radius 5 at P, and PQ = 12. What is OQ?sqrt(5^2+12^2)The tangent makes a right angle with the radius.13
D7A chord of length 16 is in a circle of radius 10. How far is it from the centre?sqrt(10^2-8^2)Half the chord is one leg.6
D8What is the radius of x² + y² − 8x + 6y = 11?sqrt(11+16+9)Add the completing-the-square constants to both sides.6
D9What is the radius of x² + y² + 4x − 2y = 20?sqrt(20+4+1)Same method, different numbers.5
D10An inscribed angle cuts an arc of 70°. What is the inscribed angle?70/2Half the arc.35

Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Find the radius first in almost every question, then answer what was actually asked: circumference, area, arc or sector.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
The area enclosed by a circular jogging path is 64π square metres. What is the length of the path, in metres?
16π

πr² = 64π gives r = 8, and the path is the circumference.

2π(8) = 16π. A common wrong answer is the radius times π, a common slip.

P2Hard
A round cheese wheel has a circumference of 18π centimetres. What is the area, in square centimetres, of its circular top face?
81π

2πr = 18π gives r = 9.

A = π(9)² = 81π. A common wrong answer squares the diameter instead of the radius.

P3Hard
A wedge cut from a circular cheese of radius 9 inches has a central angle of 80°. What is the area, in square inches, of the top face of the wedge?
18π

The whole area is 81π and the wedge is 80/360 = 2/9 of it.

(2/9)(81π) = 18π.

P4Hard
What is the radius of the circle given by x² + y² − 8x + 6y = 11?
6

Complete the square twice: (x − 4)² + (y + 3)² = 11 + 16 + 9 = 36.

r = √36 = 6. Answering 36 gives r², not r.

P5Hard
A circle in the xy-plane has equation (x − 3)² + (y + 1)² = 9. What are the coordinates of its centre?
(3, −1)

The form is (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r², so h = 3 and k = −1.

(3, −1) — the signs flip. A common wrong answer flips them the wrong way.

P6Hard
A sector of a circle of radius 6 has an area of 6π. What is its central angle, in degrees?
60

The whole circle has area 36π, and 6π/36π = 1/6.

(1/6)(360) = 60°.

P7Very
hard
In a circle with centre O, AB is a diameter and C is a point on the circle distinct from A and B. What is the measure of angle ACB, in degrees?
90

Angle ACB is inscribed in a semicircle, so it cuts an arc of 180° and is half of it.

90° wherever C sits — which is exactly why any other answer is wrong.

P8Very
hard
A tangent touches a circle with centre O and radius 5 at point P. An external point Q lies on the tangent with PQ = 12. What is the length of OQ?
13

The tangent is perpendicular to the radius OP, so triangle OPQ has a right angle at P.

OQ = √(25 + 144) = 13, the 5-12-13 triple.

P9Very
hard
A chord of length 16 is drawn in a circle of radius 10. What is the distance from the centre of the circle to the chord?
6

The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord, giving a right triangle with hypotenuse 10 and one leg 8.

d = √(100 − 64) = 6. A common wrong answer is half the chord itself.

P10Very
hard
The circular fountain plaza at the centre of a market square is modelled by x² + y² − 8x + 6y = 11, with units in metres. What is the radius, in metres?
6

Completing the square gives (x − 4)² + (y + 3)² = 36.

r = 6. A common wrong answer is r², and C is the number on the right of the original equation — both are answers to steps along the way, not the question.

P11Very
hard
A circle has centre (−2, 5) and radius 4. Write the equation of this circle.
(x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = 16

Signs flip inside the brackets and the right-hand side is r².

(x + 2)² + (y − 5)² = 16. A common wrong answer uses r instead of r²; another gets both signs wrong.

P12Very
hard
A circle of radius 12 centimetres has a sector whose arc length is 8π centimetres. What is the area of that sector, in square centimetres?
48π

The full circumference is 24π, so the sector is 8π/24π = 1/3 of the circle.

The full area is 144π, and (1/3)(144π) = 48π.

The one habit to build. The right-hand side of a circle equation is r², not r. Your class scored 47% on the circle equation, and answering 36 instead of 6 was the single most common slip.
